title: Podcast with Johannes Pollanen, Co-founder of EeroQ and a Professor of Physics at Michigan State University - Quantum Computing Report
author: Doug Finke
text:
Overview

Johannes Pollanen, co-founder of EeroQ and a professor of physics at Michigan State University, explains how EeroQ builds qubits from single electrons floating on a film of superfluid helium, and why he thinks the semiconductor chip is the only proven way to scale a quantum computer.

He covers the different kinds of quantum computer, why helium never freezes, how much helium-3 a dilution refrigerator needs, how a computation runs on a qubit, and what EeroQ’s 10,000-qubit goal means next to IBM’s plans.

This video is divided into 14 chapters as follows:

0:00 Quantum computing at a wedding

3:57 Reverse engineering quantum computing

5:15 Quality or quantity of qubits

6:23 The modalities of quantum computing

12:36 You’ll need liquid helium

19:01 Transistors and silicon

20:21 Is that thing behind you using helium-3?

26:15 How do you cool quantum systems?

31:08 How do you make more qubits?

35:15 How do you do a computation on a qubit?

40:05 Faster quantum computers

43:45 Can IBM make a useful quantum computer?

46:00 The quantum lessons of nature

48:33 Carry over question

Transcript

Quantum computing at a wedding

Mark Fielding: Disruptors and curious minds, welcome to the good ship thinking on paper. In a world increasingly vibe-coded by 20-year-olds and run by billionaires, this is where you can think for yourself about the impact of technology. Keep listening, and the algorithm can’t touch you, at least for 40 minutes. Sadly, Jeremy can’t be with us today. He’s been called away on a top secret data center mission. He signed a lot of NDAs, so the very fact I’ve mentioned this might get me disappeared. So if I’m not here next week, big AI. But we’re not talking about AI today, we’re talking about quantum computers. We’re talking about scaling quantum computers. And we’re doing this without a PhD. The idea is to combine my beginner’s mind with an expert’s mind, meet somewhere in the middle, probably near me. We’re going to be talking about trapped electrons, trapped ions, we’re going to be talking about scaling quantum computers. We’re going to be talking about the biggest challenges facing the industry and quantum mechanics at the moment. And we’re going to end with our handover question from our last guest, which is a doozy. And today’s guest is Johannes Pollanen, CSO of EeroQ. Johannes, welcome to Eric. Johannes,

Johannes Pollanen: EeroQ, yeah. Yeah.

Mark Fielding: welcome to Thinking on Paper. Thank you for thinking on paper with us. And rather than read your incredible background, I want to ask you you’re at a wedding, you’ve sat by someone you’ve never met in your life. They say, Johannes, nice to meet you. What do you do? How do you answer that question?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. I, that’s a good, it actually happens.

Mark Fielding: What’s your go to?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. My go to is you know, I start with I’m a physicist by training, but what I do for a living is try to build essentially a next generation of supercomputer using quantum physics and then follow up with like, have you ever heard of quantum computing is sort of what it starts out with. And yeah, that usually gets the ball rolling pretty quickly because people have usually heard of some amount, it’s in the zeitgeist, it’s out there and folks are thinking about it and want to know more. And yeah, that’s how I lead in and

Mark Fielding: You hope that whoever’s wedding it is, they know what your background is and they put you by somebody who can actually who’s like, not whoa. What in those situations, what is the most common go to question they ask you when you say that?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah, I often get one of two, I guess I get a handful of similar responses. I’ll often get like, physics, that was my worst subject in high school or college. Which often then heads the conversation off into the other part of my life, which is I’m also an academic. I’m a professor of physics at Michigan State University, which is where we spun out EeroQ from. We’ve developed some of the technology there and then spun it out as a company in Chicago. But often they’ll ask me, like, yeah, I’ve heard of quantum computing. I heard that, you know, when are quantum computers gonna exist, you know? Which I always think is a fun question because actually even my academic colleagues often ask me, like, when are quantum computers gonna exist? And my answer is,

Mark Fielding: Don’t they already exist?

Johannes Pollanen: Exactly. That’s what I say to them. I say they already exist. You could get on Amazon’s Braket service and connect to one via the cloud right now if you wanted to. You know, they’re not the ultimate machines that we hope to build as a species sometime, but they exist. Like we know that the basic principles work. Yeah.

Mark Fielding: Yeah, well last week we were playing quantum games using a quantum computer with moth quantum and

Johannes Pollanen: Exactly. Yeah.

Mark Fielding: that was actually kinda cool making quantum music with quantum computers.

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. And it totally works. And you can do even more. Not just playing games, right? You can people can simulate small scale molecules and you know, if you’d asked me that five ten years ago, like when are we gonna be actually simulating nature with small scale quantum computers, I don’t think many people would have predicted that we’d be doing that now, but we are.

Reverse engineering quantum computing

Mark Fielding: well let’s start there then. So on the EeroQ website you speak about reverse engineering quantum. And so I like reverse engineering things. So let’s really work backwards by going forwards. If you had a million qubit quantum computer for whatever that’s description is worth, what are you doing with it?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. I think the thing I’m most excited about is associated with chemical simulation and drug discovery. I think if you have millions or tens of millions of physical qubit machines, lots of logical qubits, then you can get to the point where problems that are intractable now in molecular simulation become very tractable. I think that’s the thing that keeps like when I get excited about it, that’s what I get excited about. You’ll also have the opportunities, you know, for cybersecurity and those kinds of things, like, you know, Shor’s algorithm kind of efforts. Those are great. I those don’t get me out of bed in the morning. I think usually it’s the things that can become life-changing, you know, for many people that I find most compelling. You know, sort of related to your first question about the, you know, what do you say to people when they ask you what you do? As I said, I’m an academic. For a long time, the work that I did in physics and in quantum science was really just for the sake of science, for trying to understand about nature. Now that we’re building technologies based on what we know, it’s the first time in my career where we can actually, you know, the things that we’re doing in the research facilities or in the academic labs or national labs in the world actually has the potential to make an impact outside of physics. You know, we can address something like, you know, curing diseases with, you know, computers that can simulate new medicines. And that I find extremely satisfying. I never was an applied person, but I understand once you realize like you can like the things that you’re doing are actually good for the world, it can be very exciting. So I think that’s the thing that I find most compelling. But I do think that for the biggest applications, you’re not just gonna get away with, you know, 100 logical qubits. You’re gonna need a lot. You’re gonna need a lot of qubits. That’s gonna be the big issue. I mean, the bigger you can make the machines, the more powerful they’re gonna be. And for those most impactful things, I think you’re gonna need big machines. Not necessarily large in space, but large in their information processing density.

Quality or quantity of qubits

Mark Fielding: So if Jeremy was here, he would ask you now on the qubit question, do you want quantity or do you want quality?

Johannes Pollanen: I think you need both. I think you really do need both. You need, you know, I can tell you a little bit more about our technology specifically, but I think the reason I like our technology is because I think we can get both. We can get high quality qubits, we can get a whole bunch of them, and we can leverage all of the most state-of-the-art advances in algorithms and error correction. And I think you need those things. I think as a community we’ve learned that none of the modalities is perfect in some sense. They all have their challenges. I think all of them can potentially be really successful, at least to some level. And but finding the one that can really like, you know, leverage sort of all of the benefits of all the different modalities, that’s the tricky part. And that’s what I really like about our system. But we can get into the details. Like I said, we have our own challenges too. Yeah. Yeah.

The modalities of quantum computing

Mark Fielding: Right. Well, let’s go back to the wedding talk. So I’m dangerous at a wedding. So modalities, I know what that means. Many people listening to Thinking on Paper will think, a quantum computer is a quantum computer. What do you mean modalities? So what are the five big modalities and where does EeroQ fit into that modality network?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. So by modality, I really just mean like what are you, what is the actual hardware that you’re gonna build the quantum computer out of? Because you can, you know, as you say, a quantum computer ultimately is a quantum computer. If you can program it the way a quantum computer should be programmed, it doesn’t matter what’s under the hood in some sense. Just like for a regular computer, it could be transistors, it could be punch cards, it could be vacuum tubes, it could be whatever you want under there. As long as it allows you to process information the same way, fundamentally, it doesn’t matter what the computer is.

Mark Fielding: Yeah, but a punch card and a vacuum tube aren’t gonna give you the same results, are they?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah, I mean, they will if you can figure out how to make them big enough, but that’s the big issue, right? Like you’re not gonna make an iPhone out of punch cards or vacuum tubes, nor are you gonna make a laptop. And so we are now facing we’re sort of in the world where there’s all these different competing ways of building computers, quantum computers that are figuring out different parts of how to do it. And but we haven’t yet found, you know, the transistor of quantum computers. So the different approaches to answer your question directly, you know, there’s the superconducting circuits of IBM and Google. There are trapped ions like the ones that Honeywell and IonQ use. There’s now you’ve probably heard, I don’t know if you all have had anyone talk to you from the neutral atom community. They’re very much like ions except without the charge. Yeah.

Mark Fielding: We’ve had Infleqtion on a couple of times.

Johannes Pollanen: Right. So Infleqtion, or atomic, logical, all of these. There’s a it’s they’re the new kid on the block in some sense. And there’s electrons trapped in semiconductors, so like the things that Intel and HRL used to do, which is now part of IBM. Those they’re using the spins of electrons in semiconductors. There are folks who are working on trying to use particles of light as the qubits, like PsiQuantum and Xanadu. And then, you know, there’s us, which we’re a little bit different, but I think we combine some of the benefits of these others. So we are an electron spin based quantum computing company. We ultimately want to use an electron and its little bit of magnetism. Each electron is kind of like a little north and south pole magnet. And you can make a quantum bit out of that magnetism. And that is what we’re working toward. And I can say more about we take those electrons and instead of having them in the silicon like the semiconductor folks do, we actually just pluck the electrons out and place them above the semiconductor control chip and hover them in vacuum, kind of like an ion trap or a neutral atom system. And the way we do that is by actually coating the underlying chip with a layer of a very thin layer of superfluid helium, and then the electrons float above that surface and are bound to it in vacuum. Yeah, it’s pretty wild, but it’s kind of amazing.

Mark Fielding: Right. Right. Of course they do. Right. We’re gonna get into this in more detail. Yeah, it sounds pretty wild.

Johannes Pollanen: You know, one of the things that I think is really important about all of these quantum technologies that I think is sometimes lost. As a species, we’ve known about quantum mechanics for like over a hundred years. But it’s only really been in my lifetime that we’ve got to the point where we can take individual quantum objects, whether they’re atoms or photons or electrons or engineer circuits that behave quantum mechanically and control their properties. You know, to like fully deterministically move them make them do what we want and then measure them. But once you have that level of control, then the engineering starts. That’s when you can really build a technology. And that’s where we are and that’s the exciting part, you know. It’s kind of amazing. Quantum mechanics was what I got excited about when I started getting into physics. But now we get to just manipulate it, you know, and do what we want.

Mark Fielding: Right. Right. You mentioned the magnetism and of the electron. Before we get I wanna go over everything you said again. Before we get to that, can you speak about magnetism, why you said the magnetism of the electron, does that matter? And then the role perhaps of magnetism beyond that in the quantum realm?

Johannes Pollanen: So for us, like you know, you imagine an electron and it’s a little charge, a little negatively charged object, but the electron has a property, a purely quantum mechanical property called spin. But spin is just a word. What it really means, what it really is physically is there’s a magnetic moment, a little north and south pole associated with you can think of each electron as having its own little bar magnet that it carries around with it. And whether those north and south poles point up and down, or whether you create superpositions of that magnetism, you know, in combinations of up and down, you can encode quantum information in that. And that’s actually the thing that, you know, the folks like Intel and HRL and the various startups, Quantum Motion, all of these companies that work on electron-based qubits, they’re utilizing that magnetism of the electron as their quantum bit. And we do the same thing.

Mark Fielding: When you said imagine each one carrying a little bar magnet around. Is that the right way to think about that? Because they’re not really spinning.

Johannes Pollanen: They’re not spinning, but there is truly a magnetism associated. You can measure, you know, there’s a magnetic interaction just like there would be for two bar magnets. It’s like the electrodynamics of that is the same. It really does boil down to that. But the spin is sort of a bad word in the sense that spin really makes it seem like there is something spinning, which, you know, that’s a very classical way of viewing the world. But ultimately we don’t. You know, sometimes people get hung up on the like we end up using language to describe things that we don’t really have intuition for. So we use words from the classical world to try to describe the quantum world. And there’s not really necessarily a one-to-one mapping on that. We understand how they work in terms of like what we measure and what we do and how we describe it mathematically, but the language often ends up being what do you say, insufficient to fully capture the underlying phenomena.

You’ll need liquid helium

Mark Fielding: I wanna build the stack. I want to understand the stack here. And I stack might not be the right word, but the ingredients, the ingredients is a better word. I want to understand the ingredients here. So you mentioned the electron, you mentioned helium. Liquid helium.

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah, liquid helium.

Mark Fielding: Had a look at liquid helium. There’s some pretty gnarly quotes about liquid helium. Is liquid helium the physical state of the element, helium at extremely low temperatures, specifically when it is cool to about minus 269 degrees, making it the coldest liquid on earth. There was another one which was what was the other. There’s something about being called the cleanest state which what’s that all about?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. So helium at so if you take we have one of our dilution refrigerators back here that goes down to, you know, very close to absolute zero. It goes to like ten millikelvin in temperature. So we build our quantum chips ultimately live inside of machines like that. And very much like what IBM and Google do for their circuits. And at those temperatures, as you say, liquid helium, helium is a gas at room temperature. But if you cool it down, like any gas, it will eventually condense and form a liquid. And helium, you just have to get very, very cold. Forms of liquid. But interestingly, helium has a very funny property. Normally, if you take a liquid and you keep cooling it, eventually it freezes. That is not true for helium. It’s true for everything, every other element known, but helium remains a perpetual liquid all the way down as cold as people have ever gotten. And there’s good reason to believe

Mark Fielding: The only one.

Johannes Pollanen: The only one, there’s one example. And it’s a purely quantum mechanical effect, actually. Because as you cool these things down, the helium atoms actually become little waves. They become quantum mechanical probability waves. And those waves overlap with one another to the extent that the system can never crystallize. And it forms instead a perpetual liquid. And it actually forms a very funny liquid called a superfluid, which flows without any viscosity.

Mark Fielding: This is where my silly questions come in and I just have to ask. Why does helium behave like that and nothing else does though? Even though you might have just answered that question.

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. There’s two I didn’t really I alluded to it, but I didn’t totally answer it. There’s two reasons. One is the helium’s crazy light. So helium other than hydrogen is the lightest of all the atoms. And so that means that when you try to you’ve probably heard of quantum zero point motion. So if you try to confine a quantum particle, it jitters around more and more. That happens more if the underlying atom is very light. So helium has a very large quantum zero point motion. So when you make it a liquid, you’re trying to essentially confine it to a single place, you know, next to its neighbors, but it doesn’t like that quantum mechanically, and so it jitters around. And so that’s one aspect that keeps it a liquid. The other one is if you bring two helium atoms close to each other, they don’t really interact very strongly with each other. They’re kind of, you know, you can’t do chemistry with helium. All of the electronic shells, if you remember from high school chemistry, the electrons on helium are completely filled up in their electronic shells. They can’t interact with one another or form bonds. And normally you need those kinds of bonds and connections to form a solid. And helium can’t do that. And it’s those two properties. It’s chemically inert and it’s very light that allow it to be a liquid forever.

Mark Fielding: Okay, and for those people who are listening not watching this, A, go to YouTube and watch it or click that button on Spotify to make it video or behind Johannes, that is happening in the chambers that we can see.

Johannes Pollanen: You have like super microphone photos. Yeah. I was just gonna say this property of superfluidity isn’t new, you know. We’ve known about it like since 1904, I think was when helium was liquefied and probably the first demonstrations of superfluidity were achieved. So it’s a state of matter that’s quite exotic and strange, but we’ve known about it as a you know, like we understand that system quite well. But there was a second part to your question, which was the cleanliness.

Mark Fielding: Yes.

Johannes Pollanen: So if let’s say that you wanna have an electron and you want it to be a qubit, so you wanna shield it from all kinds of noise and decoherence and sources of disturbance. So if you have, say, a material substrate onto which you wanna put the electron or wanna put the electron into that substrate, those things have chemical impurities and crystal defects and all kinds of vibrations and all kinds of stuff that’s terrible. So what you would really like to do is take that electron and you want to hide it away from the rest of the universe, you put it in vacuum very far away from everything. But you need to somehow hold it in vacuum. Holding an electron in vacuum is actually not so easy. But if you bring it near the surface of liquid helium, it actually naturally gets stuck about 10 nanometers above the helium surface and floats there. And then helium at those temperatures is liquid. Everything else is frozen. There’s no other atom around except helium. There’s no magnetism, there’s no charge noise, there’s none of these other things that plague other qubit platforms in the solid state. And so in that sense, it is the cleanest system for hosting one of these electronic qubits. And that’s one of the reasons we like this system. So very much the other natural qubits benefit from this as well. So for example, atoms and ions are hidden away in vacuum and then you interrogate them with lasers. And the reason that they’re so high coherence and so perfect is because they’re in vacuum very, very far away from other things.

Mark Fielding: So no lasers for you.

Transistors and silicon

Johannes Pollanen: No, yes, no lasers whatsoever. We use so actually I’ll mention the other thing that really we love about this technology is that so the other important part is that we you know, you asked this question earlier about how do you what do you need, quality or quantity? And I said both. So we kind of addressed the quality issue just now.

Mark Fielding: Yeah.

Johannes Pollanen: But the quantity issue is very important. And you have to we built quantum computers out of a variety of things and but we’ve never figured out how to build a lot of quantum bits onto a platform. In fact, in all of human history, we’ve never figured out how to make lots of anything on the computational side, except for transistors in silicon. So like the things that give you iPhones and laptops and the best supercomputers and GPUs, that is built on a semiconductor manufacturing process that only exists. We’ve only ever invented it once in all of human history. And so what we do is we actually build the underlying substrate beneath the helium out of that semiconductor material, the same way that chip builders build iPhone chips and Intel builds their quantum computers, their quantum chips, except we then combine it with this pristine helium surface with electron qubits trapped above. And I have, you know, you asked about show and tell earlier, I have one of our chips here. In the very center of this board is something about, you know, three by five millimeter chip and that can house, you know, thousands or tens of thousands of electrons. And being able to make it tiny like that is really important. You want to jam as many qubits onto a single monolithic chip as possible. And that is sort of our philosophy. You gotta get quality and quantity in as small a footprint as possible.

Is that thing behind you using helium-3?

Mark Fielding: Right. I want to lead up to that. I want to know how many qubits you can put on that and how many there are. First of all, just another helium question because at Thinking on Paper, we connect all technologies with tech, agnostic, we speak about all things. Not so long ago, we had a former NASA scientist who wants to go to the moon to mine helium three. And when we were speaking to him, one of the reasons he said that we need to go to the moon to mine helium three is because the quantum industry uses it for their cooling. Is that thing behind you using helium three?

Johannes Pollanen: Yep. Yeah, this machine uses helium three. The helium that I’m talking about for our chips is helium four. It’s the more standard one. But there is all of these behind our director of operations here is that dilution refrigerator and that thing has helium three in it. Like these cooling systems have that. You know, in an ideal world when we that system has something like 20 liters of helium three gas. And each dilution refrigerator needs that amount and you never lose it as long as you, you know, their safety is in place to kind of recollect it. Yeah, it keeps it.

Mark Fielding: Okay, it circulates around. Okay.

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah. And but it is still, you know, to make more of these, helium three is a resource that isn’t very naturally occurring. It is not so to give you a sense, you know, helium isn’t around on Earth, that’s about a part per million out of the air, because most of it when it’s in the air escapes out into outer space. It’s actually so light that it can get enough speed to get itself out of the atmosphere. So there’s about a part per million of the air is helium and about a part per million of that is helium three. So it’s a tiny fraction. And finding new sources for helium three is really important. It is extremely rare.

Mark Fielding: Very rare isotope. Well, we know there’s a show. I’ll put it in the link for our show on Helium Three because it’s all about nuclear weapons as well. So it’s a very interesting. Yeah, yeah. It’s

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah, when you said it went That’s right. Yeah, there’s an interesting history there on how low temperature physics intersected with some other innovations that we made as a species.

Mark Fielding: Right. Could you do the show and tell again? Could you hold up the chip to the camera again, Johannes?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah, absolutely. Yeah. So this is our Wonder Lake chip. Am I kidding?

Mark Fielding: Wonderlake.

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah, we named all of our chips after Lakes. Wonder Lake is a lake nearby in Chicago that we named this one after. And this one was prototyped. We design the chip and then it gets manufactured by a commercial semiconductor foundry using the standard processes that are made to like I said, make the chips in your iPhone or in your laptop. And this device was this Wonder Lake architecture was built so that we could demonstrate that we can move electrons around to do error correcting codes. So like the neutral atoms or ions, we can move our qubits around. And this was built so that we could have something like 2500 electrons on that chip.

Mark Fielding: Does twenty five hundred electrons equate to twenty five hundred qubits?

Johannes Pollanen: No, so actually our qubits ultimately will be so we can get into the details of various things, but ultimately our qubits are built from two electron objects. So we make what are called singlet triplet qubits out of two electrons. And that harkens to some of the things that the silicon spin people do, like us. We share similarity with them. And so it equates to something like, you know, half that many qubits. We don’t have thousands of qubits on this chip. This was really just designed to show that we can do the choreograph the error correction that we’ll eventually need to do. But to give you a sense our ultimate goal is to build chips that are not that much bigger than that, than the thing I just showed you and to fit, you know, millions or tens of millions of electrons and tens of qubits ultimately qubits on that kind of footprint.

Mark Fielding: So this is how we scale. This is the famous this is how we scale quantum computing.

Johannes Pollanen: This is our thesis for sure. Because again, I think, if you’re gonna set out to scale quantum computers, you have, I think, two options. You’re limited to two choices. One, use the one scaling architecture that we have ever built in all of human history, which is CMOS manufacturing and semiconductors, or you have to invent something equivalent. And the second of those sounds really hard to me, given that all of humanity has invented this once. And so I’m picking that particular battle. Like we have work to do on the quantum front and on the error correction front and all this stuff, but I think that’s a more tractable problem than inventing some other technology that we can scale to the level of, you know, ten to the ten transistors that we can do in your laptop.

How do you cool quantum systems?

Mark Fielding: Right. So we have the wafer, we have the liquid helium, we have the two electrons that are floating on that.

Johannes Pollanen: They’re floating. They’re bound. It’s actually quite so the electron is to give you a sense of why, you know, like why on earth would it get stuck there? So if you have this layer of liquid and you bring an electron nearby, the helium underneath polarizes because of the electron charge. So the helium is a dielectric. So if you bring a charge near a dielectric, it polarizes a little positive charge on the other side. And so then this electron sees a positive image charge in the liquid and gets stuck to it. It sees it and wants to go toward you know, if you have a negative charge and a positive charge, they try to get close to each other. And so the electron creates its own like fictitious positive image charge in the liquid and tries to get to it. But it can’t go in because the helium is completely inert. There are no open electronic states, so it just gets and those two things compete and it ends up finding itself, you know, 10 nanometers above the helium surface. And this is yeah.

Mark Fielding: Just gonna pull on another thread there because we spoke about dielectric fluids a few weeks ago and we were speaking about cooling AI data centers. So there’s another thinking on paper thread for everyone to pull on. But sorry, continue.

Johannes Pollanen: No, that’s a good point, actually. One of the things that we spend a lot of time one of the questions that comes up in some quantum technologies a little bit in the weeds, but how does one get heat out of the chips? You know, there can be power dissipation problems on the chip that one has to solve, particularly at scale. So we think a lot about these kinds of problems. And the dielectric helium actually is the it has at those temperatures, you know, very near absolute zero, it has the highest thermal conductivity of any known liquid, any known substance, correctly. So it pulls heat out very efficiently. So we benefit naturally from that aspect. But what was I saying? But yeah, that’s why the other thing I wanted to emphasize is all of this sounds crazy exotic. Actually, if you talk to anybody about their quantum technologies, it always sounds exotic. But all of these things have been known for a long time. So like I think the first trapping experiments of electrons above the surface of helium happened well before I was born. They happened in the boy, late sixties, early seventies.

Mark Fielding: Yeah, okay.

Johannes Pollanen: You know? And people have been building up from there. You know, it’s and it started out as just

Mark Fielding: Was that Bell Labs or something?

Johannes Pollanen: Yeah, the first experiments were done at Bell Labs and some universities. But yeah, it was it’s pretty amazing that, you know, you build up from these Bell Labs at the time had a real knack for laying the foundation for all kinds of technologies. I don’t think none of those ideas that they originally had were intended to be technologies at the time. They were really just like interesting aspects of nature that they wanted to realize and then people have built off of that, us.

Mark Fielding: You have the wafer, you have the helium, you have the electrons. At the moment, how many qubits do you have? Right. So why why is that challenge? Why are you stuck there or not? Why are you there? And why can’t one just be ten? Why can’t ten just be a hundred? And why can’t a hundred just be a thousand?

Johannes Pollanen: One. So this is now you’re getting to our challenge. Yeah. Yeah. So this idea of making qubits out of electrons on helium has been around for a while. It was actually the first proposals were made back in the nineties. But then nobody really it’s an artifact of history in the sense that, you know, people back in the nineties didn’t actually even like the first ion trap experiments were really going on then. Nobody really invented superconducting qubits or the techniques for measuring them. Silicon spin qubits didn’t exist, neutral atoms definitely didn’t exist. And so you had this community of people that had been working on electrons on helium, and then there were other communities working on quantum computing, and they just didn’t talk to each other.
